_comment: DVFS-feasible resource set. Two changes vs resources_edge_cloud_default.json,
both purely numerical -- no simulator code is touched.
(1) POWER SPLIT.  The old 'static_power' lumped always-on leakage together with
frequency-independent active power, and was charged only while a task runs.
That gave P_s/P_d ratios of 1.47 (edge_legacy) and 2.77 (edge_lowend), whose
energy-efficient frequency rho_ee = (P_s/2P_d)^(1/3) is 0.903 and >1.0: DVFS is
provably useless on 52% of the system energy.  Here the two fields are reread as
the standard three-term model P(f) = P_s + P_ind + C_ef f^m (m=3), with the
always-on P_s excluded from the scheduling objective (it can only be removed by
powering the node down) and only (P_ind, C_ef) charged per task:
static_power  := P_ind  = phi * active_power_reference
dynamic_power := C_ef   = (1-phi) * active_power_reference
phi is kept heterogeneous (0.05 .. 0.22) so servers differ in DVFS friendliness,
in the literature range around P_ind=0.05 / C_ef=1.
P_ind + C_ef == active_power_reference is preserved, so the MEAN power at rho=1
is unchanged and every rho=1 baseline number stays comparable.  It is not
bit-identical: _sample_profile_server jitters the two fields independently by
+-5%, so per-server rho=1 power moves by well under 1%.
Refs: Li/Quan JSA 2015; Xie et al. JPDC 2019; Zhang et al. Inf. Sci. 2015.
(2) TRANSIENT FAULT RATE.  The old failure_rate 6.25e-4 / 3.75e-4 per second is
2-3 orders above the literature value (1e-6 .. 1e-5 faults/s at f_max), which
made a 40-task workflow spend 60-115% of its -ln(0.9) risk budget at rho=1 and
left no admissible DVFS range at all.  Set to 1.0e-5 (edge) / 6.0e-6 (cloud),
and the DVFS sensitivity exponent d from 1 to 3 (base-10 form).
Refs: Zhu/Melhem/Mosse ICCAD 2004; Zhu & Aydin IEEE TC 58(10) 2009;
Zhao/Aydin/Zhu; Soft-error-aware DVFS cloud scheduling JSA 2018 (1e-6, d=2).
p_ind_fraction and rho_energy_efficient are documentation only -- _sample_profile_server
copies just PROFILE_FIELD_NAMES + failure_rate_exponent, so the loader ignores them.
rho_energy_efficient = (phi/(2(1-phi)))^(1/3) is the frequency below which slowing down
costs MORE energy; to make it the SAC action floor it has to be plumbed through
resource.py and the low-level action clamp.  min_rho stays at the hardware limit 0.1
because it is the f_min that normalizes the fault-rate model, not an energy bound.
(3) SPEED-POWER FRONTIER (2026-09-03).  The previous table gave edge_efficient the
HIGHEST clock (3.5 GHz) and the LOWEST power (51 W) of all five profiles, so it
strictly dominated every other profile on (max_freq_ghz, power, failure_rate,
bandwidth) simultaneously.  resource.py's own dominance audit reported it:
'server_id=8 edge_efficient dominates 19/36 servers'; 151 of the 177 dominated
pairs were cross-tier (edge_efficient over edge_lowend 90, over edge_legacy 61).
A strictly dominant profile removes the energy-latency trade-off the whole
formulation is about.  Measured on 12 episodes / 240 workflows (seeds
742000-742011) with the trained policy: it concentrates on the 10 edge_efficient
nodes, 35.2% of all task-time is then spent in server queues (a learning-free
HEFT policy on the same pool spends 8.4%), and makespan inflates to 1.75x median
/ 2.27x p90 of the contention-free HEFT reference the deadline is defined
against.  x2-multiplier workflows (which allow only 2.0x) miss ~10% of the time
while x3 never misses.  The dual multiplier cannot fix this -- there is no
faster server to escape to -- which is why lambda pinned at its ceiling.
The sharpest symptom is that the OLD table had no energy-latency Pareto front
at all.  Same 12 episodes, two learning-free policies, rho=1:
OLD:  HEFT (latency-greedy) 508.9 kJ, inflation p90 1.37
cheapest-idle (energy-greedy) 690.6 kJ, inflation p90 1.82
-> the energy-greedy policy is worse on BOTH axes; dominated.
NEW:  HEFT 572.3 kJ, inflation p90 1.46
cheapest-idle 348.1 kJ, inflation p90 1.89
-> 39% less energy for 30% more inflation; a real trade.
Both tables keep the deadline satisfiable (HEFT reaches SR=1.000 with max
inflation 1.85 OLD / 1.89 NEW) and the reliability constraint intact
(reliability_success_rate 1.000, avg R_w 0.9988 OLD / 0.9990 NEW).
The dominance was also physically inconsistent with the P(f) = P_ind + C_ef f^m
model declared above.  At rho = 1 the active power IS P_ind + C_ef, so a profile
with a higher f_max at equal-or-lower power implies a strictly smaller C_ef, i.e.
a different (better) process node on every axis at once -- free lunch.  The five
profiles are therefore re-fitted onto a monotone frontier: power at f_max grows
with f_max, and so does energy per unit of work P(f_max)/f_max, which is what
the scheduler actually trades:
profile          f_max   P(f_max)   P/f_max   C_ef (W/GHz^3)
edge_efficient    2.40      41.9      17.5          2.61
cloud_standard    3.25     243.0      74.8          6.23
C_ef rises with the tier because higher-throughput parts are wider-issue with
larger caches, i.e. more switched capacitance per cycle; this is the same
per-processor heterogeneity in C_ef used by the reference model (C_ef in 0.8-1.5
and m in 2.5-3.0 in normalized units).  No profile now dominates another: to go
faster you pay strictly more per unit of work, which is exactly the lever the
Lagrangian needs.  Cloud is also now faster than edge (it was slower before,
which inverted the standard MEC offloading trade-off); its 100 Mbps edge_cloud
link and higher power keep offloading a real decision rather than a free win.
p_ind_fraction stays inside the 0.05-0.22 literature band.  Note this does move
the SAC action floor: with simulation.dvfs_action_floor = 'energy_efficient',
edge_cloud_env.py:314 clamps rho at rho_energy_efficient, which resource.py:308
RECOMPUTES from the jittered (static, dynamic) rather than reading the field
below.  Per-profile floors go 0.2976/0.4084/0.3518/0.4784/0.5205 (cloud_fast,
cloud_standard, edge_efficient, edge_legacy, edge_lowend) -> 0.3816/0.4084/
0.4334/0.4452/0.4894, i.e. the range narrows and edge_efficient loses some DVFS
headroom.  That is a consequence of the physics, not a free parameter: a part
with a smaller C_ef has a larger P_ind share and therefore a higher rho_ee.
Absolute speeds are not comparable across resource sets,
but the deadline is multiplier x reference_heft_makespan computed on this same
pool, so it rescales with the pool and the difficulty is set by the load
DISTRIBUTION, not by the absolute clocks.
Refs: Zhang, Li, Li & Li, Inf. Sci. 379:241-256, 2017 (bi-objective energy /
reliability workflow scheduling; source of the P_ind + C_ef f^m table);
Zhang et al., Inf. Sci. 319:113-131, 2015; Li & Quan, JSA 2015;
Xie et al., JPDC 2019; Zhu & Aydin, IEEE TC 58(10), 2009.
